qualitative.3m: (1) Moat barriers: Dense ~9,800-store global NAPA hub-and-spoke auto parts network enabling <45-min commercial DIFM lift-bay delivery and 16,000+ NAPA AutoCare affiliations, paired with Motion Industries' #1 North American industrial bearings/power-transmission MRO scale and technical inventory support. (2) Empirical proof fails: While 2021-2025 median GAAP ROIC is 19.1% (aided by the 2021-2023 post-COVID boom), GAAP ROIC fell to 13.5% in 2024 and 2.3% in 2025; more critically, Incremental ROIIC across 2016-2024 was just ~1.1% pre-tax (~5.3% after-tax) as Net Invested Capital more than doubled (+$4.10B) for only +$43.5M incremental EBIT, and operating margins eroded from 8.0-8.5% (2016-2018) and 7.8% (2023) to 5.4% (2024) and ~5% adj. / 0.9% GAAP (2025) vs. 18-20% at AutoZone/O'Reilly. (3) Erosion threats: Superior commercial execution, store density, and private-label margin capture by ORLY/AZO; two-step wholesale margin squeeze when parts inflation cools while SG&A/wage costs rise; $5.04B M&A goodwill exceeding equity (-$621.5M tangible equity); Q1 2027 spin-off divesting higher-margin Motion Industries; and long-term BEV powertrain wear-part shrinkage.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (REJECTED – G3 Moat & Pricing). While GPC serves essential automotive aftermarket and industrial MRO needs with real distribution scale, empirical moat proof and pricing power fail Munger's bar: 2016-2024 Incremental ROIIC was ~1.1% pre-tax (~5.3% after-tax; negative over 2018-2024) despite +$4.1B of incremental invested capital, and operating margins compressed from 7.8-8.5% to 5.4% in 2024 and ~5% adj. (0.9% GAAP) in 2025—far below AZO/ORLY's 18-20%—with adjusted EPS falling two consecutive years ($9.33 in 2023 -> $8.16 in 2024 -> $7.37 in 2025). Calamity Tier does not apply because the margin compression and sub-hurdle ROIIC predate 2025's $741.9M pension settlement charge, goodwill ($5.04B) exceeds equity ($4.42B), and the activist-driven Q1 2027 spin-off separates higher-margin Motion Industries while leaving GPC with the weaker, BEV-exposed global automotive distribution unit.
qualitative.evidence: Multi-cycle financial history (SEC EDGAR FY2016-FY2025): Revenue grew from $15,339.7M (2016) to $23,090.6M (2023), $23,486.6M (2024), and $24,300.1M (2025), but GAAP EBIT barely moved from $1,229.3M (8.01% margin in 2016; $1,430.5M / 8.50% in 2018) to $1,272.8M (5.42% in 2024) and collapsed to $215.7M (0.89%) in 2025 on a ~$741.9M US pension settlement charge plus restructuring/credit charges. Even on an adjusted basis, 2025 net income fell to ~$1.0B ($7.37 EPS vs. $8.16 in 2024 and $9.33 peak Owner EPS in 2023) despite $175M of realized restructuring savings. GAAP ROIC averaged ~19-21% in 2021-2023 (5Y median 19.07%; 10Y median 17.95%) before compressing to 13.54% (2024) and 2.27% (2025), while 2016-2024 Net Invested Capital rose from $3,500.8M to $7,600.0M (+$4,099.2M) for +$43.5M EBIT (1.1% pre-tax ROIIC) and +$216.9M Net Income (5.3% ROIIC). Segments & 2025-2026 separation: Global Automotive (NAPA/AAG/Repco, >$15B sales, ~75-80% DIFM commercial, ~8-9% EBITDA margins) lags pure-play retail/commercial peers AZO and ORLY (~50-53% gross, 18-20% EBIT margins), whereas Motion Industries (~$9B sales, ~12-13% EBITDA margins, +6%+ YoY 2026 growth) is being carved out into an independent public company in Q1 2027 following Elliott Management's >$1B activist stake. Capital allocation & balance sheet: Serial M&A inflated Goodwill & Intangibles from $1,574.7M (2016) to $5,044.5M (2025) against $4,423.0M equity (negative tangible equity of -$621.5M) and expanded debt from $550.0M (2016) to $3,498.4M (2025; net debt $3,021.2M), pushing interest expense from $64.5M (2023) to $163.5M (2025; 1.32x GAAP EBIT coverage). Cumulative 2021-2025 Owner FCF conversion was 97.5% ($4,258.5M vs. $4,368.0M NI), but FY2025 Owner FCF ($372.1M) fell short of Dividend King payouts ($563.8M).

qualitative.3m: Local depot density and route logistics provide modest distribution scale, but post-tax GAAP ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~8-10% (well below the 12% Munger threshold) with razor-thin operating margins (~3-4%). As a bulk fuel/LPG distributor, pricing power is limited to a thin delivery markup over volatile commodity costs.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While heating fuel and LPG delivery fulfill an essential physical need, DCC operates as a high-volume, low-margin distributor with thin ~3-4% operating margins and a multi-year post-tax ROIC below the 12% hurdle (~8-10%). It lacks independent pricing power against commodity swings and faces long-term structural volume headwinds from European building decarbonization and the energy transition.
qualitative.evidence: International energy distribution and services group with over £14B continuing revenue (transitioning to pure-play DCC Energy after divesting Healthcare and Technology). Historical ROCE/ROIC hovers around 8-11% post-tax. Although cash conversion is consistently high (>90-100%), the business is constrained by commodity price pass-through dynamics and thin ~3.5% adjusted operating margins.

qualitative.3m: Regional distribution contracts and logistics density provide outsourced scale in small and emerging markets, but Inchcape possesses no structural pricing power against global OEMs (who dictate wholesale terms, hold contract cancellation rights, and can shift to direct-to-consumer/agency sales). Profitability remains vulnerable to OEM contract renegotiations and aggressive EV market discounting.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Inchcape provides outsourced vehicle distribution for global automotive OEMs (Toyota, BMW, Mercedes, BYD). However, OEMs hold the whip hand with unilateral contract renewal power, margin control, and the ability to disintermediate distributors via direct-to-consumer models, leaving Inchcape without an enduring pricing power moat.
qualitative.evidence: Pure-play global automotive distributor operating across 40+ markets following the Derco acquisition and divestment of UK retail. Operating margins sit at ~5.5-6.3%. While asset-light distribution yields high ROCE on a narrow capital base, Inchcape is structurally dependent on third-party OEM distribution agreements without proprietary toll booth protections or pricing power over vehicle MSRPs.

qualitative.3m: Pearson VUE and UK qualification awarding bodies (Edexcel) operate as secure testing and certification toll booths, but 5-year median GAAP Return on Capital/ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~10.3% (7.9% in 2021 to 11.3% in 2025, failing the >=12% Munger threshold). Furthermore, higher education courseware and learning content face long-term pricing compression and generative AI disintermediation.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While Pearson VUE computer-based testing and accredited examinations provide a strong testing toll booth, Pearson's 5-year median GAAP Return on Capital/ROIC is sub-hurdle at ~10.3% (consistently below 12% across 2021-2025), burdened by historical intangible asset acquisitions. Learning content also faces persistent pricing headwind from generative AI automation.
qualitative.evidence: Global learning and assessment provider generating ~£3.5-3.8B in revenue with adjusted operating margins improving from 11.2% in 2021 to ~17% in 2024-2025. Reported Return on Capital was 7.9% (2021), 8.7% (2022), 10.3% (2023), 10.5% (2024), and 11.3% (2025), failing the 12% multi-year hurdle required for empirical proof of moat under Gate 3b.

qualitative.3m: Brand equity and proprietary footwear design IP across UGG ($2.74B FY26 sales) and HOKA ($2.59B FY26 sales), reinforced by strict wholesale allocation and full-price selling discipline. Empirically verified by 28.5% historical median ROIC (30-35%+ in FY25-FY26), 57.9% FY25 gross margin, and 23.1%-23.7% operating margins even amid promotional industry discounting. Primary erosion threats: zero customer switching costs, fashion/silhouette cyclicality, and surging running rivals (On Holding, Salomon, Nike, Adidas).
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 20Y reduced by -10Y for footwear brand entry barriers (4_ent=1); running and casual shoe rivalry with Nike and On (4_riv=1); Asian supply-chain tariff exposure (4_sup=1); and fashion cycle substitution risk (4_sub=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While UGG and HOKA generate elite current ROIC (30-35%+) and ~23% operating margins via brand intangibles and full-price discipline, branded footwear has zero switching costs and high Mauboussin fade risk (Tier 3 baseline <=15Y) as HOKA normalizes against On Holding, Salomon, Nike, and Adidas and UGG faces fashion-cycle rotation. Deductive -5Y Macrotrend [3] haircut applies for heavy reliance on outsourced Vietnam/Asian manufacturing hit by ~20%+ U.S. tariffs, which labor-intensive shoe assembly (Macrotrend [2]) cannot economically reshore.
qualitative.evidence: FY25 net sales rose 16.3% to $4.986B (UGG $2.531B +13.1%, HOKA $2.233B +23.6%, Other $221.2M -8.6%) with gross margin expanding to 57.9% (from 55.6% in FY24) and operating income of $1.183B (~23.7% margin). FY26 net sales rose 9.8% to $5.472B (UGG $2.74B +8.2%, HOKA $2.59B +15.9%, non-core labels streamlined including Sanuk divestiture/exit) with operating income of $1.263B (~23.1% margin) and FCF above $1.1B. Historical median ROIC is 28.5% (30-35%+ recently). Management (CEO Stefano Caroti, CFO Steve Fasching) enforces full-price selling to protect brand equity despite U.S. DTC volume friction, operates essentially debt-free with $1.6B-$1.9B cash, repurchased 10.5M shares for $1.075B in FY26, and raised buyback authorization by $3.5B in May 2026 (~$5B total). Fails 15Y Munger runway bar due to zero switching costs, HOKA growth normalization amidst fierce competition, and Vietnam/SE Asia tariff concentration.

qualitative.3m: Dominant North American home-improvement duopoly (~2x Lowe's revenue with far higher sales per sq ft) creates unmatched supplier purchasing scale, proprietary/exclusive brands (Ryobi, Husky, HDX, Behr), and an integrated store plus Pro flatbed/branch network (augmented by SRS Distribution and GMS) that smaller chains and parcel e-commerce cannot profitably match on heavy, immediate-need building materials. Empirical proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 41.5% (27.1% GAAP / 56.7% tangible in FY25 post-M&A; company-reported FY25 Adjusted ROIC 25.7%), positive full-cycle incremental ROIIC (>15% after tax even including $23B+ of recent M&A at a housing trough), and gross margins held steady at ~33.0%-33.7% through lumber, tariff, and wholesale-mix pressures. Primary erosion threats: structural margin and ROIC dilution as lower-margin specialty Pro wholesale distribution grows in mix, prolonged high mortgage rates suppressing big-ticket remodel turnover, and e-commerce encroachment in lighter hardware SKUs.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -10Y for big-box home-improvement rivalry with Lowe's (4_riv=1); Pro contractor wholesale buying power (4_buy=1); and building material tariff/commodity supply volatility (4_sup=1); unreplicable big-box real estate and heavy-freight logistics provide strong structural insulation.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. North America's indispensable home-improvement retail and Pro building-materials leader, anchored by scale economies shared across ~2,300 big-box stores and >1,250 SRS/GMS specialty trade branches serving continuous repair/maintenance on an aging housing stock. Physically insulated from AI disruption and online parcel economics, with diversified sourcing managing tariffs and high-rate housing turnover muting growth cyclically rather than terminally. CAP set conservatively at 15Y to reflect US store saturation and ROIC/margin fade toward wholesale Pro distribution. Balance sheet passes baseline hurdles (3.49x LT debt/NI, 3.39x net debt/NI, 8.66x EBIT/interest at cycle trough, 91.6% 5Y FCF conversion), with buybacks prudently paused since March 2024 to pay down M&A debt and commercial paper, though $32.7B of goodwill leaves negative tangible book equity and post-dividend deleveraging warrants monitoring. [5-10Y g: R&R/Pro volume 2.5% + pricing/ticket 2.0% + SRS/GMS cross-sell mix 1.0% - wholesale mix/tariff drag 0.5% + normalized buybacks 1.5%]
qualitative.evidence: 10-year SEC EDGAR financials (FY2016-FY2025) and 2026 interim filings verify exceptional multi-cycle capital efficiency and cash conversion despite a frozen US housing turnover backdrop. Revenue compounded from $94,595M (FY16) to $164,683M (FY25), dipping only 3.0% from the FY22 pandemic peak ($157,403M) to FY23 ($152,669M) before rebounding via Pro expansion and turning positive organically in 1H 2026 (Q1 2026 sales $41.8B, comps +0.6%; Q2 2026 sales $47.9B, comps +1.7%). Operating margins ranged from 13.8%-15.3% pre-2024 before stepping down to 13.49% (FY24) and 12.69% (FY25) due to lower-margin SRS/GMS wholesale mix, M&A intangible amortization, and housing turnover deleverage; consolidated gross margin held tightly near ~33.0%-33.7% across 2025-1H 2026. GAAP ROIC ranged from 34.9%-55.7% across FY16-FY24 and printed 27.14% in FY25 (5Y median 41.53%; company Adjusted ROIC 25.7% in FY25, 25.4% in interim 2026), while tangible operating ROIC remained 56.74% in FY25. Owner FCF totaled $126,804M across FY16-FY25 against $129,459M Net Income (97.9% 10Y conversion; 91.6% 5Y conversion), with capital-light maintenance needs (FY25 capex $3,679M vs D&A $3,514M, ~2.2% of sales) and minimal SBC ($522M, 0.3% of sales). Owner EPS compounded at 6.84% over 10 years ($6.73 in FY16 to $16.69 FY22 peak; $14.23 in FY25 trough), with clear peak-to-peak recovery visibility as turnover normalizes and SRS/GMS synergies scale. Following major Pro acquisitions—HD Supply (2020), SRS Distribution (2024), and GMS Inc. (FY25, ~$5.5B EV)—goodwill/intangibles rose from $12,061M (FY23) to $32,673M (FY25) (yielding -$19,860M tangible equity despite GAAP equity rebounding to $12,813M), and LT debt peaked at $51,365M (FY24) before declining to $49,397M (FY25) ($1,389M cash; 3.49x LT debt/NI; 8.66x EBIT/interest). Management kept share buybacks paused from March 2024 through 1H 2026 to prioritize dividend stability ($9,152M in FY25) and commercial paper/debt reduction; CEO Ted Decker took a temporary medical leave in August 2026 with tenured insiders Ann-Marie Campbell and CFO Richard McPhail assuming interim oversight.

qualitative.3m: #2 position in the US big-box home improvement duopoly behind Home Depot, backed by $86B-$92B purchasing scale, supply-chain density, private-label depth, and physical store/distribution reach for bulky and urgent building materials. Historical 10Y median ROIC is 28.5% with FY2026 trailing ROIC of ~24.8%-26.8% (though optically elevated by $(9.9B)-$(14.2B) shareholders' deficit from buybacks) and 11.2%-12.5% operating margins. Fails Gate 3b on autonomous pricing power >= inflation and recent incremental returns: #2 price-follower with a DIY-heavy mix facing transparent SKU price competition from Home Depot, Amazon, and regional chains plus commodity pass-through dynamics in lumber/building supplies. In FY2024-2026, inflation-adjusted pricing/volume power stalled (FY2026 comparable sales guided flat after +0.6% Q1 and +0.2% Q2) while GAAP operating margin compressed from 12.5% (FY2024) to 11.8% (FY2025) to 11.2% guidance (FY2026E), and ~$10B of 2025 Pro wholesale/installation M&A (ADG >$1B; FBM $8.8B) diluted margins with flat-to-lower GAAP EBIT ($10.47B FY24 vs ~$10.30B FY26E).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT – G3 Moat & Pricing). Although Lowe's passes Gates 1-2 as an essential US home-maintenance retailer and holds #2 scale economies in the home-improvement duopoly (3a = Scale economies shared), it lacks autonomous pricing power >= inflation and exhibits deteriorating incremental returns. Heavily DIY-skewed and trailing Home Depot in Pro share, Lowe's acts largely as a retail price-follower on cross-shopped tools/appliances and a pass-through merchant on commodity building materials. Amid sticky inflation, comparable sales have stalled (FY2026 guidance cut to flat after +0.6% Q1 and +0.2% Q2) while GAAP operating margins compressed from 12.5% (FY2024) to 11.8% (FY2025) to 11.2% guidance (FY2026E), with ~$10B of debt-funded 2025 Pro acquisitions (ADG and FBM) diluting margins and failing to lift GAAP EBIT above FY2024 levels.
qualitative.evidence: Financial Track Record & Cash Conversion: FY2024 net sales $83,674M, GAAP operating income $10,466M (12.51% margin), net earnings $6,957M, operating cash flow $9,625M less CapEx $1,927M = ~$7,698M FCF (~111% conversion). FY2025 (ended Jan 30, 2026) net sales $86,286M, GAAP operating income $10,153M (11.77% margin), net earnings $6,654M, non-GAAP FCF ~$7.7B (~116% conversion). FY2026 guidance (updated post-Q2 after Q1 +0.6% comps on $23.1B sales and Q2 +0.2% comps on $26.0B sales): ~$92.0B sales (down from $92B-$94B), flat comps (down from flat to +2%), 11.2% GAAP operating margin (11.6% adjusted), ~$1.6B net interest expense, ~$11.75 GAAP EPS ($12.25 adjusted), and up to $2.5B CapEx. Capital Efficiency & Pricing Power: Workbook 10Y median ROIC is 28.5% and 2026 trailing ROIC hovers near ~24.8%-26.8%, though book invested capital is shrunk by shareholders' deficit ($(14,231)M in FY2024; $(9,917)M in FY2025) from prior buybacks. Pricing power is constrained by #2 DIY-heavy positioning behind Home Depot, cross-retailer price transparency, housing turnover lock-in, and commodity pass-through dynamics, yielding flat nominal FY2026 comps and ~130 bps of GAAP margin compression since FY2024. M&A, Capital Allocation & Balance Sheet: Seeking catch-up penetration in the $250B Pro market, Lowe's deployed ~$10B in 2025 on Artisan Design Group (>$1B, mid-2025; builder interior finishes installation) and Foundation Building Materials ($8.8B cash, closed Oct 2025 via $9.0B bridge facility and debt; >370 interior building product branches), diluting operating margins and lifting long-term debt (excl. current) from $32,901M (FY24) to $37,490M (FY25) — 5.63x FY25 net earnings, with FY26E GAAP EBIT/interest coverage tightening to ~6.4x.

qualitative.3m: Extensive store network (B&Q, Castorama, Screwfix) and own-brand sourcing provide retail purchasing scale, but 5-year median GAAP ROIC is deeply sub-hurdle at ~5-7% (far below the 12% threshold). Big-box DIY retail suffers from intense price competition, heavy lease liabilities, and lack of customer lock-in.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). Kingfisher operates home improvement retail across the UK, France, and Poland, but generates structurally weak capital returns with multi-year ROIC hovering at only 5-7% and thin 3.5-6.5% operating margins. Highly exposed to cyclical housing turnover and consumer DIY pullbacks, it lacks genuine pricing power against discounters and online rivals.
qualitative.evidence: Multi-banner home improvement retailer with >2,000 stores across 8 European countries generating ~£13B in revenue. Group operating margins fluctuate between 3.5% and 6.5%. ROIC consistently prints in the 5-7% range, trailing its ~8% cost of capital. Substantial operating lease obligations and heavy store overhead prevent high-return capital compounding.

qualitative.3m: Rural store density and farm-savvy customer service create local convenience switching barriers in secondary/tertiary markets, but TSCO lacks structural pricing power above inflation. Passing on price increases leads directly to unit volume contractions, traffic declines, and customer cross-shopping at Walmart, dollar stores, local farm co-ops, and e-commerce (Chewy/Amazon).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT – G3 Moat & Pricing). Specialty rural lifestyle retailer with strong brand recognition and high ROIC (~14-18%), but lacks genuine pricing power above inflation. Unit volumes and transaction counts stall when prices rise, as seen in flat comparable store sales (+0.1% FY24, +1.2% FY25, -1.0% to 0% FY26 guidance) and stagnant net income plateaued at ~$1.10B across 2022-2025. Operating margins compressed to 8.0-8.3% due to rural wage inflation and SG&A pressures.
qualitative.evidence: FY2024 revenue of $14.88B and net income of $1.10B; FY2025 revenue of $15.52B and net income of $1.10B (zero net income growth across 4 consecutive years). Comp store sales moderated from pandemic highs to +0.1% in FY24, +1.2% in FY25, and guided -1.0% to flat in FY26 (Q3 2026 at +0.4%). Free cash flow conversion remains weak at ~58% in FY24 ($637M FCF / $1,101M NI) and ~68% in FY25 ($741M FCF / $1,096M NI), well below the 80% threshold due to $675M-$700M annual capex. Balance sheet carries $1.83B in long-term debt plus >$3.5B in operating lease liabilities across 2,390+ stores.

qualitative.3m: Scale economies shared via massive direct procurement of fresh, responsibly sourced ingredients and industry-leading restaurant throughput ($3.2M+ AUV across 4,000+ company-owned locations). Insurmountable unit cost advantages allow CMG to deliver high-protein, 1.5-lb+ entrees at accessible price points that fragmented fast-casual peers cannot replicate at scale. Moat proved by multi-year GAAP ROIC consistently exceeding 20% (and operating ROIC >45%) alongside successful cumulative price realization passing through ingredient and wage inflation. Primary erosion threats: brand fatigue / portion perception backlash, unit-level labor cost escalation, and aggressive copycat fast-casual concepts.
qualitative.4n: Fatal-Flaw Cap triggered (Final CAP = 10Y, REJECT): structural food-service wage inflation and labor shortages under Macrotrend #2 (4_sup=2) alongside fast-casual competitive rivalry (4_riv=1) and consumer price elasticity (4_buy=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Chipotle has built an exceptional fast-casual brand with high throughput and unit volumes, it operates an entirely company-owned restaurant footprint of 4,000+ units employing ~120,000 hourly workers without a franchise royalty buffer. The business faces an unhedged terminal headwind under Macrotrend 2 (Demographic Aging & Labor Scarcity), where structural food-service wage inflation and labor shortages compress restaurant-level margins (falling from 27.4% to 23.3% in 2026). Under the Mauboussin Rule of Secular Resilience, an active headwind on manual labor intensity caps the competitive advantage period at CAP <= 10 years, failing the 15-year Munger longevity threshold.
qualitative.evidence: Chipotle grew revenue from $6.0B in 2020 to $11.3B in 2024 and $11.9B in 2025, with operating income of $1.94B (16.2% operating margin). High capital efficiency is demonstrated by multi-year GAAP ROIC of 20-47%, supported by $3.2M+ average unit volumes (AUV) and sub-2-year cash payback on new builds across 4,042 restaurants. Pristine balance sheet with zero funded debt (only operating lease liabilities of $5.1B) and ~$1B+ in cash and short-term investments. FCF conversion tracks 80-85% of net income ($1.15B FCF on $1.4B net income). However, the 100% company-operated store model leaves Chipotle directly exposed to accelerating hourly labor inflation (e.g. California AB 1228 $20/hr minimum wage), requiring continuous labor investments that compressed restaurant-level margins from 27.4% to 23.3% in 2026. Executive leadership transition to CEO Scott Boatwright in late 2024 has necessitated deliberate margin concessions to protect transaction traffic and resolve consumer portion-size pushback, underscoring secular labor and consumer sensitivity limits.

qualitative.3m: Domino's operates an entrenched scale economies shared moat: high store density ('fortressing') cuts delivery radiuses and transit times, while vertically integrated regional supply chain dough/ingredient centers pass procurement efficiencies to franchisees. National scale funds an advertising powerhouse (6% royalty/ad contribution) and digital dominance (37M+ active loyalty members). Empirical proof: historical ROIC consistently 30-50%+ and ability to lift core promotional pricing ($5.99 to $6.99) while maintaining positive order counts. Primary erosion threats: third-party delivery aggregators (DoorDash, Uber Eats) disintermediating customer relationships and fast-food discounting wars.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -10Y for third-party delivery aggregator substitution (4_sub=1); fast-food promotional rivalry (4_riv=1); and consumer price elasticity (4_buy=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT). While Domino's franchise economic engine is highly cash generative (FY2025 FCF of ~$672M, >110% GAAP net income conversion) and interest coverage is 5.27x, it fails Munger's peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet test. Decades of debt-funded share repurchases and whole-business securitizations have driven book equity into a -$3.90B deficit (negative tangible equity, triggering an automatic Gate 6 red flag) with $4.81B in long-term debt against FY2025 net income of $601.7M (8.0x net debt / net income, double the <= 4.0x ceiling). The capital structure relies continuously on the kindness of debt markets to roll over securitized tranches, leaving equity vulnerable to credit freezes.
qualitative.evidence: FY2025 operating results demonstrate strong underlying unit economics: Total revenues of $4,940.0M (+5.0% YoY), operating income of $954.0M (+8.5% YoY), and GAAP net income of $601.7M (+3.0% YoY). Free cash flow converted cleanly at ~$671.5M-$680.1M (Operating cash flow $792.1M less capex of $120.6M, representing ~112% of net income). Historical ROIC exceeds 35-40% across cycles driven by asset-light franchising (over 20,000 stores globally, ~98% franchised) and cost-plus supply chain centers. However, capital structure violates Gate 6 balance sheet standards: Long-term debt stood at $4,810.7M at FY2025 year-end (up from $3,825.7M in FY2024), resulting in Net Debt / Net Income of ~8.0x (far above the <= 4.0x ceiling). Total liabilities exceed total assets by $3.90B, leaving stockholders' deficit at -$3.90B due to cumulative leveraged share repurchases. Annual interest expense of $181.1M yields interest coverage of 5.27x, offering minimal safety margin during economic or credit downturns. Because this high-leverage recapitalized structure is permanent management policy rather than a temporary shock, Calamity Tier is inapplicable.

qualitative.3m: Supply chain and global marketing purchasing power create insurmountable scale economies shared with franchisees, enabling unmatched value menu pricing (e.g. $5 Meal Deal, McValue) while extracting 15%+ percentage rent and royalty tollbooths on top-line sales. Competitors cannot replicate McDonald's prime corner-lot physical real-estate footprint or supply contracts. Empirical proof: 10-year median ROIC of 30.3% and consistent >45% operating margins across cycles. Primary erosion risk: low-income consumer traffic sensitivity to cumulative post-COVID menu inflation and QSR value price wars.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 30Y reduced by -10Y for QSR value discounting rivalry (4_riv=1); low-income consumer price resistance (4_buy=1); and franchisee labor/food supply pressures (4_sup=1); unreplicable commercial real-estate footprint provides strong structural insulation.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Irreplaceable global QSR real-estate and franchise royalty tollbooth operating 40,000+ locations across 100+ countries. Massive supply chain scale economies shared with franchisees enable unmatched value pricing while collecting contractually formula-indexed percentage rents and royalties (>45% operating margin). Insulated from macrotrends via localized sourcing, kiosk/mobile automation (210M+ digital loyalty users), and inflation-indexed rent streams. Balance sheet structured for peace of mind: $40B debt is supported by 7.8x interest coverage and non-displaceable commercial real-estate cash flows; negative book equity is an artifact of cumulative historical buybacks that is steadily normalizing. [5-10Y g: net unit growth 2.0% + comparable sales/price 2.5% + mix/digital 1.0% - franchisee support margin drag 0.5% + net share repurchases 1.5%]
qualitative.evidence: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 30.3% and operating ROIC of 33.7%, consistently exceeding 23% in all years since 2016 (peaking at 34.1% in 2021). Multi-year FCF conversion of 90.6% (2025 Owner FCF of $8.19B vs Net Income of $8.56B). Peak-to-peak Owner EPS compounded at 8.7% CAGR from $5.44 in 2016 to a record $11.95 in 2025. Systemwide sales exceed $139B across 40,000+ restaurants (approx. 95% franchised). High-margin franchise royalties and property rental income generate operating margins >45% ($12.39B EBIT in 2025). Long-term debt of $39.97B is supported by 7.83x interest coverage (EBIT $12.39B / Interest $1.58B) and contractual real-estate rental agreements. Negative accounting equity (-$1.79B in 2025) is an artifact of historical treasury share repurchases and has narrowed from -$8.21B in 2019 without external solvency risk.

qualitative.3m: Global fast-food franchisor with iconic brand intangibles (Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes, Firehouse Subs) across 31,000+ units. The ~98% franchised model captures menu price inflation directly via percentage-of-sales royalties. qualitative.note: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT). While Restaurant Brands International operates an asset-light, highly cash-generative fast-food franchise model (>100% FCF conversion) with entrenched everyday consumer habits (Tim Hortons morning coffee ritual, Burger King value dining), it structurally fails the Munger peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet standard. Legacy debt from 3G Capital's debt-financed acquisitions leaves QSR burdened with $15.7B in total debt and $14.5B in net debt against $776M-$1,021M of GAAP net income (14.3x to 18.7x Net Debt/NI, far exceeding the <=4.0x ceiling; 10.0x Net Debt/FCF). EBIT interest coverage is persistently depressed at 3.4x to 4.2x (4-year median ~3.86x), failing the >5.0x through-the-cycle requirement. With annual dividends ($1.1B) consuming ~75% of FCF, the company cannot organically retire debt and remains perpetually reliant on debt market refinancing ('kindness of strangers').
qualitative.evidence: Asset-light global restaurant franchisor (~98% franchised across 31,000+ units in 100+ countries). Free cash flow conversion is strong at >100% of GAAP Net Income ($1.45B FCF vs $776M Net Income in FY2025; $1.30B FCF vs $1.02B Net Income in FY2024) with low maintenance capex ($200-265M on $8.4-9.4B revenue). Tangible Operating ROIC is >50%, but reported GAAP ROIC is mediocre at 8.8% to 11.3% (5Y median ~9.7%) due to $17.5B in capitalized acquisition goodwill and brand intangibles. Structural Gate 6 failure is absolute: Total debt is $15.70B, Net debt is $14.54B, and Stockholders' Equity is $3.63B against negative tangible equity (-$13.86B). Net Debt to Net Income stands at 18.7x in FY2025 (14.3x in FY2024; 11.2x in FY2023; 13.2x in FY2022) and Net Debt to FCF is 10.0x, massively violating the 4.0-year Owner Earnings ceiling. EBIT interest coverage has failed the 5.0x threshold in every year of the cycle (FY2022: 3.67x, FY2023: 3.44x, FY2024: 4.06x, FY2025: 4.23x; 4-year median 3.86x). Dividends of $1.1B annually consume almost all free cash flow, leaving zero organic capacity for debt amortization.

qualitative.3m: Global store density, proprietary ethical coffee sourcing/roasting infrastructure, and the Starbucks Rewards digital ecosystem (~34M+ active US members with substantial prepaid stored-value float) create high customer repeat frequency and scale advantages over independent cafes. Empirical proof includes a 10-year median ROIC of 22.8% and gross margins near 68-70%. Primary erosion threats include value-conscious customer pushback on premium pricing, beverage preparation complexity eroding throughput, rapid low-cost automated rivals in international markets (e.g. Luckin in China), and store-level labor friction.
qualitative.4n: Fatal-Flaw Cap triggered (Final CAP = 10Y, REJECT): barista labor scarcity, unionization wage pressures, and green coffee cost inflation under Macrotrend #2/#5 (4_sup=2) alongside consumer price resistance to premium drinks (4_buy=1) and specialty coffee rivalry (4_riv=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). While Starbucks commands an iconic global beverage brand and habitual daily ritual, it faces severe structural headwinds under the 5-Macrotrend filter. Demographic aging and labor scarcity (Pillar 2) create persistent operational bottlenecks and wage inflation across its ~400,000 store workers that cannot be automated without degrading the handcrafted coffeehouse proposition. Furthermore, geopolitical and low-cost competitive displacement in China (Pillar 3) broke its primary international growth vector, forcing a retreat to a licensed JV model. Combined with balance sheet fragility (-$8.1B shareholders' deficit from historic debt-funded buybacks and ~$15B in long-term debt), Starbucks fails the Munger durability bar for a 15+ year predictable compounding runway.
qualitative.evidence: FY2025 revenue was $37.2B with operating income compressing to $2.9B (7.9% operating margin) before recovering toward $2.5B+ net income in FY2026 under Brian Niccol's 'Back to Starbucks' turnaround. 10-year median ROIC is 22.8%, proving historical brand power and returns on capital. However, traffic declines in 2024-2025 demonstrated pricing elasticity limits for $7+ handcrafted drinks. In China, relentless low-cost competition from Luckin Coffee forced a structural conversion of retail operations into a licensed JV in 2026. The balance sheet carries ~$14.6B-$15.0B in long-term debt against net income of $1.86B-$2.53B (debt/net income ~5.8x-7.8x) and a total stockholders' deficit of $(8.1B) resulting from aggressive debt-funded share repurchases.

qualitative.3m: Global franchisor scale advantage (~98% franchised across ~60,000 restaurants) anchored by iconic Lindy consumer brands (KFC, Taco Bell). Massive collective marketing budgets ($1B+) and supply chain purchasing power create high barriers against independent restaurant operators. Demonstrated pricing power through menu price hikes and digital upsells outpacing food-away-from-home CPI without volume destruction. Primary erosion threats include fast-casual competition, third-party delivery fee friction, and franchisee margin compression from minimum-wage inflation.

Brands possesses high-quality franchise economics across KFC and Taco Bell with excellent cash conversion (FCF >95% of NI), its capital structure fails Munger peace-of-mind standards: long-term net debt of ~$10.5B represents ~6.7x normal owner earnings ($1.56B FY2025 net income, well above the <=4.0x threshold), interest coverage is thin at ~4.4x EBIT/interest (below the >5.0x minimum), and multi-year debt-funded share repurchases have created a -$6.17B stockholders' deficit (severely negative tangible equity), triggering the disqualifying financial engineering red flag.
qualitative.evidence: FY2024 revenue of $7.55B, operating profit of $2.40B, net income of $1.49B, and FCF of ~$1.43B. Repaid $675M credit facility with proceeds but returned $1.8B to shareholders via buybacks and dividends in 9M 2026, maintaining long-term debt at ~$10.5B against cash of ~$450M. qualitative.3m: Foodbuy procurement scale delivers food and supplies at costs unobtainable by regional competitors, passing savings to clients while contract escalators protected margins during 2022-2024 inflation with >96% retention.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -10Y for institutional contract procurement rivalry (4_riv=1); client budget scrutiny (4_buy=1); and food/labor input cost inflation (4_sup=1); unmatched Foodbuy scale provides strong structural insulation.

qualitative.evidence: Consistently achieves 18-22% GAAP ROIC over multi-year cycles (median 19.1%). Owner FCF conversion exceeds 120% of net income ($2.43B FCF vs $1.87B NI in FY25). Foodbuy purchasing power aggregates massive volume, establishing an insurmountable cost advantage over regional peers.

qualitative.3m: While Sodexo possesses global catering scale, its multi-year GAAP ROIC (6-8%) and operating margins (3-5%) consistently fall far short of the 12% hurdle. Lacks the food procurement scale and execution efficiency of Compass Group, with returns diluted by facilities management.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC & Proof of Moat). Despite global contract catering presence, 5-year GAAP ROIC sits at ~6-8% and operating margins at 3.3-4.7%, well below the 12% hurdle. Lags peer Compass Group substantially in North American procurement scale, operating efficiency, and contractual pricing leverage.
qualitative.evidence: Reported GAAP ROIC was 6.1% in FY23 and 7.7% in FY24, with operating profit margins hovering between 3.3% and 4.7%. Even after spinning off high-margin voucher business Pluxee in early 2024, core on-site catering and facilities management fail to demonstrate economic moat returns.

qualitative.3m: Dominant US on-demand local delivery network (~67% market share) demonstrating clear pricing power via take-rate expansion from 11% to over 13.5% through DashPass subscription scale (18M+ members) and high-margin merchant advertising without losing customer volume.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -10Y for food-delivery platform rivalry (4_riv=1); merchant fee resistance (4_buy=1); and gig-courier labor regulation (4_sup=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 6 (Cash & Fortress Balance Sheet, REJECT). While DoorDash possesses a dominant US food delivery network effect (~67% market share) and pricing power via take-rate expansion, reported cash flows are an accounting mirage heavily distorted by massive stock-based compensation ($1.10B in FY24, $1.05B in FY25, exceeding cumulative GAAP net income). The company lacks a multi-cycle peak-to-peak earnings track record (GAAP profitable only since FY24) and has taken on $3.3B in debt to fund aggressive cross-border and software acquisitions (Deliveroo, SevenRooms), failing Munger's real cash conversion and balance sheet standards.
qualitative.evidence: FY24 revenue $10.72B (+24%), operating loss $(38)M, GAAP net income $123M, FCF ~$1.8B, SBC $1.10B. Relies on subsidiary divestments and listings (e.g. Talabat in UAE) rather than organic self-funding economic moats.

qualitative.3m: Premium tire brand equity and specialized engineering know-how, but commodity passenger and commercial replacement tires face fierce price competition from low-cost Asian imports while auto OEMs squeeze margins, capping 5-year median GAAP ROIC at 11.1% (below the 12% hurdle).

qualitative.3m: High-value prestige tire positioning and Formula 1 sponsorship create brand recognition, but GAAP ROIC of ~6-7% (obscured by non-GAAP adjustments excluding €4.5B+ buyout intangibles) fails the 12% hurdle; vulnerable to automotive OEM price pressure and raw material inflation cycles.

Lacks durable pricing power above raw material inflation cycles.
qualitative.evidence: Reported GAAP net income of ~€470-500M on total invested capital of ~€7.7B (equity €5.76B + net financial debt €1.93B) results in GAAP ROIC of ~6.1-6.5% and ROE of ~8.1%, far below the 12% threshold. ADM is a price-taker on commodity crush margins (soybean crush, corn wet milling, ethanol) and cannot raise prices independently of global market supply and demand. 5-year median ROIC (~5-7%) and 10-year median ROIC (9.5%) consistently fail the 12% threshold.

Structurally lacks pricing power above inflation.
qualitative.evidence: Historical ROIC: 2020: 3.9%, 2021: 5.4%, 2022: 7.2%, 2023: 7.3%, 2024: 3.7%, 2025: ~2.8%; 10-year median ROIC is 9.5%, consistently failing the 12% hurdle. Operating margins range from 1.8% to 4.3% across the cycle. While ADM generates substantial revenue ($85B-$100B+) and operates an essential global agricultural logistics network, profits are fundamentally tied to spot crush margins and grain supply dynamics rather than proprietary pricing power. FCF is highly volatile due to massive working capital swings tied to commodity price cycles ($1.2B in 2024 vs $4.2B in 2025). Furthermore, internal control material weaknesses and SEC/DOJ investigations over intersegment profit shifting to mask Nutrition segment underperformance resulted in a $40M SEC settlement in January 2026.

Margins remain hostage to industry crush spreads and volatile working-capital swings.

July 2025 acquisition of Viterra ($10.6B total consideration including $5.34B stock and $3.55B debt absorption) expands scale in grain handling and origination but increases capital intensity and leverage while leaving the core price-taking commodity economics unchanged. Bunge cannot unilaterally raise prices above global market-clearing levels without immediate customer defection.

Growth has been heavily reliant on acquisitions (e.g., Vrumona in the Netherlands, Norkhald, San Giorgio), increasing leverage and execution risk without establishing durable global moat barriers.

qualitative.3m: Rural small-format store density (~20,000 locations) provides convenience in small towns, but the company lacks pricing power against Walmart and branded CPG suppliers. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has fallen to ~9.2% (6-8% in FY24-FY25), well below the 12% threshold, with negative incremental ROIIC over the last cycle. Primary erosion threats include Walmart's superior scale/omnichannel reach, hard discounters (Aldi, Dollar Tree), shift toward low-margin consumables, and inflation squeezing core low-income consumers.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). Rural discount retailer lacks pricing power above inflation; selling branded packaged goods to financially stretched low-income consumers forces severe margin compression when input costs rise. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has deteriorated to ~9.2% (FY24-FY25 ROIC ~6-8%), well below the 12% threshold, with negative incremental ROIIC over the past cycle as $2B+ in invested capital yielded lower operating profit ($2.2B vs $3.2B in FY21). Intense everyday low price competition from Walmart and hard discounters prevents sustained economic profit compounding.
qualitative.evidence: Dollar General operates ~20,000 small-format stores across 47 US states, serving rural areas where 75% of Americans live within 5 miles of a store. However, consumables represent over 80% of net sales, leaving the company exposed to low gross margin items (~20-25%) while higher-margin seasonal/home merchandise has lagged. Operating margin compressed from 8.6% in FY21 to 4.2% in FY24 before recovering modestly to ~5.1% in FY25 ($2.2B operating profit on $42.7B sales). 5-year GAAP ROIC has dropped below the 12% hurdle (FY21: ~14.5%, FY22: ~13.5%, FY23: ~9.2%, FY24: ~6.1%, FY25: ~6.8%, 5-year median: ~9.2%). Incremental ROIIC across the 2021-2025 cycle is negative. The business model possesses neither pricing power >= inflation nor defensible excess returns above cost of capital.

qualitative.3m: Dollar Tree attempts a scale economies shared model in small-box discount retail, but lacks an insurmountable cost advantage against Walmart (over 30x larger scale) and cross-border ultra-discount platforms (Temu, Shein). Proof of moat fails: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5% (against the 12% hurdle). The company lacks pricing power >= inflation: breaking its $1.00 price point to $1.25 triggered traffic drag, while multi-price tiering ($3-$7) directly exposes it to fierce competition from Walmart everyday low prices with zero defensible barriers.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 8.5% < 12%, REJECT). Discount variety retailer lacks structural pricing power and fails empirical proof of moat. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 8.5% falls well short of the 12% threshold. Moving away from its signature $1.00 fixed-price format to $1.25 alienated core budget shoppers, while the multi-price expansion ($3, $5, $7) directly collides with retail behemoths (Walmart) and cross-border ultra-discount platforms (Temu, Shein) without an insurmountable cost advantage.
qualitative.evidence: Financial Track Record: 10-year / 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.5%, consistently failing the 12% hurdle. Operating margins historically hovered around 5-8%, expanding slightly to ~8.3-8.5% on continuing operations post-Family Dollar separation. FCF generation historically fluctuated ($1.1B in FY2025 on continuing operations) but burdened by continuous store renovation, multi-price format conversions (Dollar Tree 3.0), and lease obligations. Segments & Business Model: Following the July 2025 sale of Family Dollar to Brigade Capital and Macellum Capital for $1.007B in cash (a staggering loss on the $8.5B paid in 2015), the company operates primarily the Dollar Tree banner (>8,000 stores). Assortment is roughly 45-50% consumables (food, snacks, health and beauty, cleaning supplies) and 50-55% variety/seasonal merchandise. Pricing Power & Moat Dynamics: Dollar Tree possesses zero switching costs and no pricing power above inflation. The breaking of the $1.00 price point to $1.25 in 2021-2022 generated customer resistance and foot traffic declines. The multi-price expansion ($3-$7) strips away the format's simplicity and brings Dollar Tree into direct competition with Walmart, Dollar General, and factory-direct cross-border e-commerce (Temu, Shein). M&A & Capital Allocation: The 2015 debt-funded acquisition of Family Dollar for $8.5B destroyed billions of dollars in shareholder value through massive goodwill impairments, operational dysfunction, and eventual fire-sale divestiture in 2025 for $1.007B. Even on standalone operations, capital reinvestment yields sub-hurdle returns.

High-margin retail media (Walmart Connect, $6.4B run-rate) and marketplace fees increasingly subsidize core retail pricing. Proof: 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 18.9% and operating ROIC of 25.7%. Primary erosion risks include Amazon digital delivery density, deep discounter expansion (Aldi), and distribution center wage inflation.

qualitative.3m: Tesco is the undisputed UK grocery market leader (~28% market share) with massive purchasing power, Clubcard loyalty ecosystem, and Booker wholesale network. However, it operates in a fiercely competitive UK grocery market where it lacks unconstrained pricing power >= inflation. To prevent market share leakage to hard discounters (Aldi, Lidl), Tesco is forced to match Aldi on 600-700+ core staple lines ('Aldi Price Match') and use Clubcard prices defensively. Full-cycle GAAP ROIC across the total invested capital base (including store leases) averages ~7.8%, falling well short of the 12% compounder hurdle.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC ~7.8% full-cycle vs 12% hurdle, REJECT). UK supermarket market leader constrained by perpetual price competition with Aldi/Lidl; forced into defensive Aldi Price Match on staple goods, resulting in wafer-thin operating margins (~4.0-4.3%) and sub-hurdle full-cycle capital returns.
qualitative.evidence: While unadjusted accounting ROIC excluding leases appears higher over recent inflationary years, Tesco's multi-year full-cycle ROIC on total capital employed is ~7.8%. Retail operating margins hover around 4.1-4.3%. The business relies on heavy 'Save to Invest' cost reductions to offset wage and input inflation rather than exercising autonomous pricing power above inflation.

qualitative.3m: Entrenched niche brand leadership across consumer staple categories (Arm & Hammer, Trojan, First Response, Batiste, Waterpik, TheraBreath) where #1/#2 market shares and retail shelf space deter direct competition from conglomerates. Demonstrated pricing power through raw material inflation cycles with gross margins sustained around 44-45% and 10-year median ROIC ~16.8% (FY24-FY25 GAAP ROIC ~13.5-14.0%). Key erosion risks include private-label penetration in value laundry and retail customer concentration.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -5Y for retail customer concentration and buyer bargaining power (4_buy=1); #1/#2 niche brand leadership provides strong structural insulation.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Resilient consumer staples portfolio of focused #1/#2 brands anchored by Arm & Hammer. Pricing power demonstrated across inflationary cycles with gross margins at 44-45%. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends with FCF conversion >100% and conservative ~2.7x net debt to net income. [5-10Y g: volume 1.5% + price 1.5% + mix/reinvestment 2.0% - margin drags 0.0% + buybacks 1.5%]
qualitative.evidence: 10-year median ROIC of 16.8% (FY24 ~14.0%, FY25 ~13.8%). FY25 net sales reached $6.20B with operating income of $1.17B (18.9% margin) and FCF of ~$1.1B on net income of $741.5M (>140% FCF conversion). Net debt of ~$2.0B easily serviceable via ~2.7 years of net income with interest coverage at ~12.3x.

qualitative.3m: Colgate commands a dominant ~41.4% global value share in toothpaste and ~32.4% in manual toothbrushes across 200+ countries, reinforced by massive Lindy brand awareness, ubiquitous shelf-space distribution, and strong dental professional endorsements. Hill's Pet Nutrition adds a high-margin science-based moat driven by veterinarian recommendations and therapeutic formulas. Demonstrated pricing power through repeated mid-single digit price increases passing through commodity inflation while maintaining or expanding market share. Empirical moat proof: 10-year median GAAP ROIC of 35.6%, operating ROIC exceeding 100%, and gross margins near 60%. Primary erosion risks include private label encroachment in basic tiers and retail channel consolidation.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -5Y for global oral care and premium pet food competitive rivalry (4_riv=1); dominant worldwide market share (>41%) and professional endorsements provide unassailable structural insulation.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Unrivaled global oral care franchise commanding >41% worldwide toothpaste market share alongside Hill's high-margin science-based pet nutrition. Demonstrated pricing power across multiple inflationary cycles with multi-year GAAP ROIC averaging >35%. Fully insulated from 5 macrotrends with local supply chains and non-discretionary daily consumable habits. Robust balance sheet with 12x+ interest coverage and Net Debt repayable in <1.6 years of Owner FCF. [5-10Y g: volume 1.5% + price 2.0% + mix/reinvestment 1.5% - input cost drag 0.5% + buybacks 1.0%]
qualitative.evidence: 10-year financial history demonstrates extraordinary capital efficiency: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 35.6% (operating ROIC >100%), gross margins consistently 59-60%, and Owner FCF conversion averages >120% of GAAP Net Income ($3.48B Owner FCF vs $2.13B GAAP NI in 2025). As of Q3 2026, organic sales grew 3.6% (+1.7% volume, +2.0% price) with Hill's organic sales up 5.7% and toothpaste global value share steady at 41.4%. Balance sheet carries $6.87B long-term debt against $1.29B cash (net debt $5.58B), generating $3.31B EBIT with $267M interest expense for 12.4x interest coverage, well above safety thresholds. 62 consecutive years of dividend increases.

qualitative.3m: Category leadership and Lindy brand recognition across core staples (Clorox bleach, Pine-Sol, Glad, Kingsford, Hidden Valley). Multi-cycle median ROIC of 18.2% and gross margin recovery back to ~44.5% demonstrate brand pricing power, but commoditized chemical formulations face persistent private-label substitution pressure (Great Value, Kirkland).
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 15Y reduced by -5Y for mature household staples competitive rivalry (4_riv=1); and private-label chemical/commodity substitution across bleach and trash bags (4_sub=1).
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 4 (CAP = 10, REJECT). Mature, heavily US-centric household staples portfolio with flat-to-negative multi-year organic volume growth and severe private-label substitutability across core categories (bleach, trash bags, cat litter). Under Macrotrend 5 (Structural Inflation & Cost of Capital), persistent commodity input cost volatility (resin, chlor-alkali) and elevated refinancing costs on ~$4.0B of debt collide with private-label price ceilings, capping the competitive advantage period below the 15-year hurdle.
qualitative.evidence: 10-year median ROIC ~18.2%. Revenue has compounded at <2% CAGR over FY15-FY25, with organic volume frequently flat to negative. Gross margin collapsed from 45% to ~36% during the 2021-2023 inflationary shock, requiring aggressive pricing actions to recover to 44.5%, which triggered volume elasticity and trade-downs to store brands. Over 80% of sales remain concentrated in the saturated domestic US market, leaving limited runway for value-accretive capital deployment. Failed M&A diversification in vitamins/supplements (RenewLife/VMS) resulted in major goodwill write-downs and subsequent divestment.

qualitative.3m: No structural moat archetype. Kimberly-Clark operates in commoditized consumer tissue and personal care categories with zero customer switching costs and high private-label retailer penetration. The company cannot sustain price hikes above raw material (wood pulp, polymer resins) inflation without volume erosion and market share loss to store brands, exemplified by its complete exit from the Canadian consumer Kleenex business in 2023. Top-line 10-year revenue CAGR of under 1% significantly lags cumulative inflation.
qualitative.note: Rejected at Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing). Kimberly-Clark lacks a defensible moat archetype ('None') and fails pricing power ('N'). In commoditized tissue and personal care categories with zero switching barriers, price increases to recover volatile raw material (pulp, resin) costs trigger volume losses to lower-priced private label and store brands. 10-year sales CAGR (<1%) severely trails inflation, and margins remain cyclical to input cost spikes.
qualitative.evidence: 10-year net sales hovered between $18B and $20B (CAGR <1% from 2015 to 2025), failing to keep pace with >30% cumulative inflation and reflecting chronic real volume stagnation. Gross margins are volatile and exposed to commodity cycles, falling from ~37% in 2020 to ~30.5% in 2021-2022 during input cost inflation. Complete exit from the Canadian consumer facial tissue market (discontinuing Kleenex) in 2023 demonstrated inability to pass through costs against private label. Infant care (Huggies) faces long-term demographic volume headwinds from declining birth rates alongside fierce competition from Procter & Gamble and retailer store brands.

qualitative.3m: Lacks a structural moat archetype ('None'). Consumer tissue and basic hygiene products face intense private-label competition from European grocers. Multi-year GAAP ROIC sits chronically below the 12% hurdle (~6.5-8.5%), and price increases persistently lag volatile pulp and energy feedstock cost spikes, causing periodic operating margin compression.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (3a = None, 3b = N, REJECT). European hygiene and tissue manufacturer lacking structural moat defenses against supermarket private-label penetration. 10-year average GAAP ROIC hovers around 6.5-8.5% (failing the 12% hurdle), and margins experience extreme volatility during pulp and energy cost inflation cycles.
qualitative.evidence: Spun off from SCA in 2017. Segments include Health & Medical (TENA, Leukoplast), Consumer Goods (Lotus, Tempo, Zewa, Cushelle), and Professional Hygiene (Tork). Operating margin compressed to 5.5% in 2022 during pulp/energy spike before recovering to 12.4% in 2025. Long-term GAAP ROIC averages 6.5-8.0%, failing the Munger moat capital efficiency test.

qualitative.3m: Lacks a structural moat across the consolidated group ('None'). While Adhesive Technologies has industrial application stickiness, Consumer Brands (Persil, Schwarzkopf, Dial) faces persistent private-label erosion and weak volume growth. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 8.72% (well below the 12% threshold) burdened by heavy historical M&A goodwill, with organic sales growth driven by price increases against flat or negative volumes.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (3a = None, 3b = N, REJECT). German consumer goods and adhesives conglomerate whose 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 8.72% fails the 12% threshold. Consumer Brands unit chronically loses volume when attempting to pass on chemical and energy inflation, while accumulated M&A goodwill permanently depresses consolidated returns.
qualitative.evidence: Reported GAAP ROIC of 6.30% (FY22), 6.99% (FY23), 10.45% (FY24), and 10.72% (FY25) yields a 5-year median of 8.72%. Goodwill and intangibles of EUR 17.3B on EUR 20.5B equity. Organic volume growth was negative in 2023 (-4.2% price vs negative volume) and flat in 2025 (+0.9% organic entirely price-led).

qualitative.3m: Consolidated 5-year median GAAP ROIC is depressed to 7-10% (failing the mandatory 12% hurdle) due to the $16.6B Mead Johnson acquisition goodwill, subsequent multi-billion pound write-downs, and severe infant formula litigation liabilities. Outside of core OTC health, price increases in home hygiene triggered volume declines and market share losses to private label.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (3b = N, REJECT). Global consumer health and hygiene portfolio carries brand intangibles, but consolidated 5-year GAAP ROIC of 7-10% fails the 12% threshold, permanently scarred by the disastrous $16.6B Mead Johnson acquisition and subsequent write-downs. Price hikes in non-health categories resulted in negative volumes, demonstrating limited pricing power.
qualitative.evidence: Acquisition of Mead Johnson in 2017 for $16.6B bloated balance sheet with goodwill and intangibles, triggering successive multi-billion pound impairments and depressing consolidated ROIC below 10% for nearly a decade. Core OTC brands (Nurofen, Strepsils, Gaviscon) have strong margins, but volume elasticity across Essential Home and infant nutrition litigation overhang led to multi-year underperformance and CEO turnover.

qualitative.3m: Lindy brand power and grocery shelf real estate across North America Retail (Cheerios, Pillsbury, Betty Crocker, Nature Valley) and Pet (Blue Buffalo). However, brand equity has steadily commoditized against aggressive private-label store brands, fresh perimeter alternatives, and price-sensitive consumer defection, preventing price realization above inflation without severe volume loss.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Pricing Power & Proof of Moat, REJECT). General Mills lacks pricing power >= inflation: price increases during post-pandemic inflation triggered sustained organic pound volume contractions and market share losses to private-label alternatives across cereal, snacks, and refrigerated dough. To defend volume in FY25-FY26, management was forced to step up trade promotions and consumer value investments, causing organic net sales to contract (-2% in FY26) and ROIC to moderate below the 12% threshold (9.3%-11.3% in FY25-FY26).
qualitative.evidence: FY24-FY26 financial results demonstrate structural pricing elasticity constraints: FY24 reported net sales down 1% with negative volume; FY25 organic sales flat to down with heavy promotional discounting; FY26 organic sales down 2% and reported net sales down 5% to $18.4B. ROIC moderated from 11.3%-12.3% in FY24 to 9.3%-11.3% in FY25, failing the sustained >= 12% cycle hurdle. Free cash flow contracted from $2.53B in FY24 to $2.29B in FY25 and $1.63B in FY26. Blue Buffalo pet food segment has slowed from premiumization tailwinds to category normalization, failing to offset center-aisle grocery volume declines.

qualitative.3m: Brand equity in staple packaged protein and shelf-stable foods (SPAM, Skippy, Jennie-O, Planters, Hormel Black Label) creates shelf presence, but lacks pricing power to outrun commodity cost swings. Competitors and private-label store brands readily arbitrage shelf space in packaged meats and nuts. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has deteriorated to ~8% (FY21 10.1%, FY22 9.5%, FY23 7.7%, FY24 8.5%, FY25 6.1%), well below the 12% hurdle. Pricing actions trigger retail volume elasticity and market share erosion.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC < 12% and lack of pricing power >= inflation, REJECT). While Hormel possesses recognizable consumer protein and pantry brands (SPAM, Skippy, Planters, Jennie-O), it operates as a price-sensitive packaged food processor unable to pass through sustained input cost inflation without suffering volume declines. 5-year median GAAP ROIC has sunk to ~8% (dropping to 6.1% in FY25), well below the 12% threshold. Capital allocation was further impaired by the debt-financed $3.4B Planters acquisition, which diluted returns on capital and triggered $234M in non-cash impairments in FY25.
qualitative.evidence: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structural capital efficiency erosion: GAAP ROIC steadily fell from 13.1% in FY20 to 10.1% in FY21, 9.5% in FY22, 7.7% in FY23, 8.5% in FY24, and 6.1% in FY25 (5-year median ~8.1%, far below the 12% Munger hurdle). Operating margins compressed from ~10.3% in FY21 to 5.48% GAAP (8.4% adjusted) in FY25. In FY21, Hormel acquired Planters from Kraft Heinz for $3.4B funded by ~$3.2B in senior notes, expanding long-term debt from negligible levels to $2.8B-$2.9B. The acquisition diluted corporate returns and required $234M in Q4 FY25 non-cash asset impairment charges. Attempts to raise prices across Retail triggered consumer pushback and elasticity-related volume contractions, proving absence of pricing power ahead of inflation. Jennie-O turkey operations remain subject to biological and commodity cycles (avian influenza). FCF conversion has fluctuated widely ($762M in FY20, $1.01B in FY24, and dropping to $535M in FY25).

qualitative.3m: While Kraft Heinz holds iconic brand intangibles across condiments, cheese, and packaged meals (Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia, Oscar Mayer), the economic moat fails empirical verification. 5-year median GAAP ROIC of ~5.2-6.8% falls dramatically short of the 12% hurdle (and tangible ROIC fails the 15% threshold). Pricing power above inflation is absent: price increases across 2022-2024 resulted in severe volume contraction (-2.1% volume/mix in FY2024, -3.4% organic sales in FY2025) as price-sensitive consumers migrated to private-label store brands, forcing heavy promotional rollbacks and marketing reinvestments. Structural moat erosion is compounded by retailer bargaining power (Walmart, Kroger, Aldi) and center-aisle grocery disintermediation.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC = 5.2-6.8% < 12%, lack of pricing power; REJECT). Despite possessing household heritage food brands (Heinz, Kraft, Philadelphia), Kraft Heinz fails the empirical proof-of-moat test with multi-year GAAP ROIC severely below the 12% hurdle. Attempts to pass through input cost inflation via list price hikes triggered immediate volume contractions (-2.1% in FY2024, -3.4% organic sales in FY2025) and private-label market share losses in core center-store categories, disproving pricing power.
qualitative.evidence: Financial Track Record: 10-year median ROIC is 6.8%, with 2023-2025 annual ROIC lingering between 4.9% and 5.7%, well below the 12% cost of capital benchmark. In FY2024, net sales fell 3.0% (organic sales -2.1%) with persistent negative volume/mix across North American retail. In FY2025, organic net sales contracted -3.4%, driven by consumer pushback and private-label share gains in cheese, meats, and shelf-stable meals. FCF generation remained positive ($2.96B in 2023, $3.16B in 2024, ~$3.7B in 2025), but capital returns remain depressed by a legacy goodwill and intangible base that suffered a $15.4B write-down in 2019 and recurring subsequent impairments. Balance Sheet & Leverage: Net debt stands at ~$17.5B-$18.5B ($21.2B total debt vs $3.7B cash in FY2025), representing ~4.7x net debt to normalized net income, exceeding the conservative fortress threshold. Competitive Dynamics: Private label penetration in US center-aisle grocery exceeded 20-23% in 2024-2025, as major grocery retailers (Walmart Great Value, Kroger, Aldi) narrowed the quality gap and expanded price differentials, stripping Kraft Heinz of pricing independence.

qualitative.3m: Global Lindy snack brand portfolio (Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Ritz, LU, Toblerone) backed by massive direct-store delivery and global retail distribution networks. However, proof of moat fails empirical hurdles: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is ~7-10.8% (consistently below the 12.0% hurdle) due to a heavy invested capital base burdened by $24.0B+ of goodwill and $16.0B+ of acquired intangibles. Furthermore, steep cocoa and packaging cost inflation highlighted clear pricing power boundaries, as aggressive price increases induced volume/mix contraction (-1.0% in FY24 with sustained volume elasticity in FY25) and retail pushback.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3 (REJECT). Proof of Moat fails empirical hurdle: 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 10.8% in workbook data and ~6-9% on reported GAAP figures across 2020-2025, consistently missing the mandatory 12.0% threshold. Heavy goodwill and intangibles from historical acquisitions (Kraft spin-off, Cadbury, Clif Bar, Chipita) dilute returns on capital. Furthermore, pricing actions to pass through 50-year-high cocoa costs led to negative volume elasticity (-1.0% volume/mix in FY24 and persistent volume pressure in FY25), proving pricing power cannot outpace severe input cost spikes without customer volume loss. Downstream gates bypassed per strict waterfall.
qualitative.evidence: Mondelez International generates over $36B in net revenue from iconic snack food brands (Oreo, Cadbury, Milka, Ritz, belVita, Philadelphia). Despite strong brand recognition, historical GAAP ROIC has consistently trended between 5% and 11% (2020: ~6.5%, 2021: ~7.3%, 2022: ~5.2%, 2023: ~8.9%, 2024: ~9.2%, 2025: ~5.4%), yielding a 5-year median of 10.8% (or lower on reported GAAP), failing the mandatory 12.0% hurdle. Invested capital (~$45B) is heavily weighted by $24.0B of goodwill and over $16B of other intangibles. In FY24 and FY25, organic revenue growth (+4.3%) was driven entirely by pricing, while volume/mix turned negative (-1.0% in FY24 with continued elasticity in FY25). FY25 reported operating income dropped ~44% to $3,548M and net income declined to $2,451M under peak cocoa cost pressures. Total debt stands at $21.2B ($19.1B net debt), representing ~7.8x FY25 net earnings.

qualitative.3m: Category-captain shelf dominance and iconic heritage brands (McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's, Cholula) create formidable intangible barriers. Supermarket retailers rely on McCormick to design, stock, and manage entire spice aisles. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100% (GAAP ROIC ~9.6-10% reflects $8.6B goodwill/intangibles from RB Foods and Cholula acquisitions). Successfully passed through 20%+ cumulative pricing over 2021-2024 with volumes recovering to positive growth in 2024-2025. Primary erosion risks are private-label trade-down in commoditized basic spices if retail price gaps widen excessively, and customer consolidation in quick-service restaurant B2B solutions.
qualitative.4n: Initial CAP 25Y reduced by -5Y for private-label basic spice competitive rivalry (4_riv=1); category captaincy and proprietary condiment formulations provide exceptional structural insulation.
qualitative.note: Passes all 6 gates. Global leader in spices, seasonings, and flavors with unmatched grocery category captaincy and iconic brands (McCormick, Frank's RedHot, French's, Cholula). Proved pricing power through 20%+ cumulative price realization during the 2021-2024 inflation cycle. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 100%, and balance sheet deleveraging continues steadily (Net Debt / NI = 3.8x, interest coverage 5.5x). Fully insulated from AI and technology disruption. [5-10Y g: organic volume 1.5% + price/mix 2.0% + margin expansion/deleveraging 1.5% + bolt-on M&A/buybacks 0.5%]
qualitative.evidence: FY2025 revenue reached $6.84B with operating income of $1.07B (15.7% operating margin). Tangible ROIC consistently exceeds 100%, while GAAP ROIC median is 9.6% due to $8.6B of acquired goodwill/intangibles. 2025 Owner EPS reached a new peak of $2.97 (surpassing prior peak of $2.80 in 2021 and $2.62 in 2019), confirming peak-to-peak compounding. Free cash flow conversion averaged 89.3% in FY2025 ($694M Owner FCF vs $789M Net Income) and >90% over 5 years. Total long-term debt reduced from $4.44B post-RB Foods acquisition in 2017 to $3.11B in 2025. Net debt of $3.01B is repayable in 3.81 years of net income, and EBIT/interest coverage is 5.46x. 40 consecutive years of dividend increases.

qualitative.3m: Saputo possesses significant dairy processing and distribution scale in Canada, the US, and internationally, but its product portfolio (fluid milk, cheese blocks, dairy ingredients) is heavily commoditized. It faces strong countervailing buyer power from national grocery chains and intense competition from private-label alternatives. Realized selling prices fluctuate with volatile dairy benchmark spreads (e.g. US block/barrel cheese) rather than independent pricing power.
qualitative.note: Rejected at Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Saputo operates in a structurally low-margin, commoditized dairy processing sector with severe private-label competition and no unilateral pricing power. Multi-cycle ROIC of 4-7% consistently fails the 12% economic moat hurdle.
qualitative.evidence: Operating margins have hovered tightly between 4.0% and 6.0% over FY2020-FY2025. 5-year median ROIC sits at ~5.2%, well below the cost of capital and the 12% Munger moat threshold. Substantial capital deployed on international acquisitions (Murray Goulburn in Australia, Dairy Crest in the UK) has failed to generate economic profits, proving the lack of structural pricing power.

qualitative.3m: Brand intangibles across US grocery shelf staples (Jif peanut butter #1, Folgers coffee #1 retail ground, Milk-Bone #1 dog treat, Smucker's fruit spreads, Uncrustables) provide widespread retail distribution, but fail to generate economic moat protection. Pricing power is severely constrained by intense private-label store brand competition in spreads and coffee, acute customer concentration with retail giants (Walmart accounts for roughly 33% of sales), and direct exposure to volatile green coffee bean commodity cycles. Capital efficiency is chronically sub-hurdle, with 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~8.5% (and recent GAAP ROIC <2%), well below the required 12% threshold.
qualitative.note: Fails Gate 3b (Proof of Moat & Pricing Power, REJECT). 10-year median GAAP ROIC of ~8.5% (and low-single-digit ROIC following the $5.6B Hostess acquisition) falls far short of the mandatory 12% hurdle across the cycle. Despite leadership in pantry staples (Jif, Folgers) and pet snacks (Milk-Bone), the business lacks true pricing power above inflation due to severe customer concentration (Walmart represents roughly one-third of sales), intense private-label competition in spreads and coffee, and volatile green coffee input commodity swings. The massive ~$2.9B goodwill/intangible impairment on Hostess Brands underscores chronic value destruction and inability to compound capital at high incremental returns.
qualitative.evidence: Multi-cycle financial track record demonstrates structurally inadequate capital efficiency: 10-year median GAAP ROIC is ~8.5%, with peak pandemic-era ROIC reaching only ~7.0% (FY2021) and falling to low single digits (~1.8% or negative) in FY2025-FY2026 following $2.9B in non-cash goodwill and trademark impairments on Hostess Brands. Operating margins historically range between 12-14% during normal periods but experience significant volatility from commodity costs (green coffee, peanuts) and supply chain shocks. Revenue concentration is acute, with Walmart accounting for approximately 33% of total net sales, limiting bargaining leverage. The $5.6B Hostess acquisition completed in FY2024 increased debt to ~$7.0B (debt/EBITDA ~4.4x post-deal) with subsequent multi-billion impairment charges confirming significant capital misallocation and inability to generate >12% incremental ROIIC.
